I wrote the 8 test statistics to `experiment2/model_loop/iter_0/critique/test_stats/`. I haven't run the posterior-predictive harness; the pipeline does that. As a sanity check, I ran each statistic on the observed data and on one random yes/no dataset. Each returned a finite float in about 0.01 s, well under the 0.3 s per call allowed.

Each one targets something the incumbent's mechanism (rules, intervals, uniformly drawn strays) could plausibly get wrong:

| Statistic | What a discrepancy would mean |
|---|---|
| `hull_gap_interior_yes_rate` | In sets spanning 40 or more, people say yes to targets far from every example (and sharing no final digit) more or less often than the interval-plus-stray model predicts. |
| `near_miss_in_last_digit_rule_sets` | In sets where every example has the same final digit, people say yes to close numbers that break the rule (within 2 of an example) more than the model predicts. |
| `decade_match_outside_range_contrast` | Outside the set's range, people favour targets in the same tens decade as an example; the model has no notion of decades. |
| `majority_digit_rule_with_outlier_yes` | In 4-example sets where 3 share a final digit, the odd one out weakens the rule more (lower) or less (higher) than the model's reliability belief predicts. |
| `shared_contained_digit_nonfinal_yes` | People extend "contains digit d" to targets that share no final digit with the examples more than the model predicts. |
| `arithmetic_relation_target_excess_v2` | People favour targets that are a sum, difference, double or half of the examples. The model has no such relations. |
| `single_example_magnitude_gradient` | With a single example, "yes" falls off with distance more steeply than the model predicts. |
| `late_minus_early_yes_rate` | The yes rate drifts across the session, which a model with no time dependence can't produce. |

In the earlier experiment's critiques, almost no statistic came back significant (the best had p ≈ 0.09). This round's data are different: noisier sets that often contain one odd-one-out number, and an overall yes rate of 0.36. So the statistics focus on sets with an odd-one-out and on similarity by size and shared digits. I also added a note to my memory file listing these 8 so later rounds don't propose them again.

As a sanity check, I ran each statistic on the observed data and on one random yes/no dataset. Each returned a finite float in about 0.01 s, well under the 0.3 s per call allowed.

Each one targets something the incumbent's mechanism (rules, intervals, uniformly drawn strays) could plausibly get wrong:

| `decade_match_outside_range_contrast` | Outside the set's range, people favour targets in the same tens decade as an example; the model has no notion of decades. |
| `majority_digit_rule_with_outlier_yes` | In 4-example sets where 3 share a final digit, the odd one out weakens the rule more (lower) or less (higher) than the model's reliability belief predicts. |
